profile.campus: Iron Mountain Northern Virginia / Manassas campus (142 acres)
profile.reading:
Iron Mountain Incorporated (NYSE: IRM) is a publicly traded REIT headquartered in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, whose core business is physical and digital records management; its data center division was built substantially through a January 2018 acquisition of IO Data Centers. Per Wikipedia's account of that deal, the acquired IO facilities were in New Jersey, Ohio, and two Arizona sites; this registry has found no primary source tying Iron Mountain's Virginia campus to that acquisition, so it is treated as a ground-up Iron Mountain build rather than legacy IO Data Centers infrastructure.

This building, VA-1, at 11680 Hayden Road, Manassas, Virginia, is part of Iron Mountain's 142-acre Northern Virginia data center campus in Prince William County. Per the operator's own site, the full campus (which it describes simply as its "Northern Virginia" or "Manassas" campus, without a separate proper-noun brand) currently comprises seven operational data centers, with a planned buildout of nine to ten buildings totaling more than 2,000,000 square feet and 400-plus MW of capacity, and Iron Mountain has separately acquired an adjacent 40-acre parcel for two further buildings totaling roughly 150 additional MW.

VA-1 specifically carries 12.4 MW of IT capacity across roughly 167,959 gross square feet, arranged in six data halls of about 11,000 square feet each on traditional raised flooring, described by the operator as a "Tier III design" with Block N+1 configuration. Referenced certifications include FISMA HIGH, FedRAMP Ready, SOC 2 Type II, and ISO standards. No year-opened date or an independently verified Uptime Institute tier certificate number was located for this building in sourcing to date.

Iron Mountain trades on the New York Stock Exchange under ticker IRM and files with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission under CIK 0001020569, structured as a real estate investment trust. Records management remains the company's larger, founding business line by facility count; the data center segment is reported separately in Iron Mountain's public filings as a smaller but faster-growing division. Prince William County, where VA-1 sits, has become one of the most active data center construction markets in Northern Virginia alongside neighboring Loudoun County, driven by proximity to the same regional fiber and power infrastructure.

reading.body:
Iron Mountain's VA-1 facility in Manassas carries 12.4 MW of IT capacity, a modest footprint within Virginia's published data center fleet. The campus sits in Prince William County, one of the two most active data center markets in Northern Virginia, with 330 mapped facilities statewide and only 25 publishing capacity figures; at rank 26 by published megawatts, VA-1 falls outside the state's top tier. The operator describes it as Tier III design with Block N+1 configuration across six raised-floor data halls, though no independent Uptime Institute certificate was located to confirm this tier rating.

The facility qualifies for federal workloads under FISMA High and FedRAMP Ready certifications, and attests SOC 2 Type II compliance for customer data handling. At a standard assumption of 74 kW per rack for colocation workloads, 12.4 MW translates to roughly 167 racks; at 100 kW per rack for early-stage AI training densities, approximately 124 racks. The building is not positioned as a hyperscale training campus but as a hardened government-adjacent colocation facility, part of Iron Mountain's broader records management business model adapted to data center use.

Iron Mountain's full Northern Virginia campus plans 400-plus MW across nine to ten buildings, with an adjacent 40-acre parcel holding an additional roughly 150 MW. VA-1 is the published smallest unit reported so far from this campus, suggesting larger operational buildings in the portfolio. The company is a NYSE-listed REIT whose data center division is smaller than its founding records management business but growing faster; Virginia now anchors a material portion of this division's footprint, reflecting the state's position as a regional hub for both government compliance and cloud infrastructure.
